opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a distinction I think about a lot, because I lived through both of them pretty closely.

If you look at roughly 2010 to 2020, the defining pattern was: pick a problem, collect a dataset for it, design an architecture, and train a model that becomes very, very good at that one thing. ImageNet for image classification, sequence-to-sequence models for machine translation, AlphaGo for Go, and the work we did on StarCraft with AlphaStar. Each was a big achievement, and deep learning kept proving it could beat the previous state of the art almost everywhere it was applied. But the recipe was still bespoke. Every new problem meant, more or less, a new model, new data, sometimes a new team. The knowledge didn't transfer much from one project to the next, other than the techniques themselves.

What changed, and it built gradually from things like language modeling at scale, is that we found a recipe where you train one model on an enormous, very broad distribution of data, mostly next-token prediction, and that single model can do many tasks it was never explicitly trained for. You don't train a translation model anymore. You train a general model, and translation, coding, summarization, question answering and reasoning come out of the same set of weights. Then you specialize it, or you just prompt it.

So for me the key shift is from specialist models to generalist models. In the earlier era the question was "can deep learning solve this task?" Now the question is more "what can this one model not yet do, and how do we close that gap?" That changes how research is organized as well. It's much more about scaling, data, post-training, and evaluation of one system than about crafting many separate systems.

There's also a continuity I don't want to lose. A lot of what makes today's models work, like sequence modeling, attention, and reinforcement learning from things like games, came straight out of that earlier decade. And I think some of the lessons from that era, especially from reinforcement learning, where agents improved by acting and getting feedback, are coming back now as we try to get these general models to reason, plan, and act more autonomously. So it's less two separate eras and more the first one setting the stage for the second.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task-specific models with a general model, but does not identify reusable algorithms as the earlier era’s locus of generality.

r002.rationale: It describes language modeling at scale, mostly next-token prediction, as the recipe for one model to perform many tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the 2010 to 2020 decade was really about proving that deep learning works, one domain at a time. You'd pick a problem, say speech recognition or image classification or machine translation, and you'd build a model specifically for it. You'd design the architecture, you'd collect a dataset for that exact task, and you'd train a network that only knew how to do that one thing. If you wanted to solve a different problem, you started over. Even something like AlphaGo, which was a huge moment, was a system built for Go. It wasn't going to play StarCraft, and it certainly wasn't going to write an essay.

What changed, and I'd put the inflection somewhere around the transformer and then the large language models that followed, is that we stopped building a model per task and started building a model that you then point at tasks. You train once on an enormous amount of data, mostly text at first and now increasingly images, audio, code, and so on, and the same set of weights can translate, summarize, answer questions, write code, things nobody explicitly trained it for. The task is specified at inference time, through the prompt, rather than baked in at training time through the dataset and the architecture.

I think the deeper shift underneath that is where the effort goes. In the deep learning era, a lot of the cleverness was in architecture design and in the inductive biases you chose for a problem. In the general model era, the architecture is almost boring. It's roughly the same recipe everywhere. The cleverness moved to scale, data, and the training process, and to understanding what emerges when you push those. And that's genuinely surprising to a lot of us who were in the field earlier, because we assumed you'd always need specialized structure. It turns out that if you give a fairly generic model enough data and compute, generality is what you get, and that reframes what the research questions even are.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task-specific systems with a generic trained model whose same weights can handle many tasks, locating generality in the model rather than in task-specific designs.

r002.rationale: It mentions large language models, text training data, and prompting tasks, but does not explain language modeling as the abstraction that lets one model address many tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the main distinction is where the generality lives. In the deep learning era, we had a fairly general recipe: you could take a neural network, train it with gradient descent, and apply that recipe to vision, speech, or translation. That was incredibly powerful. But you would typically train a different model for each task, with a particular dataset and a particular objective.

With general models, we’re moving toward having that breadth within a single model. You train it once, and then you can ask it to do many different things, including things you didn’t explicitly formulate as tasks during training. The interface becomes much more about providing instructions or examples than collecting a new dataset and training a new network.

So there’s a lot of continuity—it’s still deep learning. But the unit we’re building has changed from a system that solves one problem to a model that can be adapted to many problems. And that changes both how we do research and how people can use the technology.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the reusable deep learning recipe with generality residing within a single trained model.

r002.rationale: It says one model can handle many tasks, but does not identify language modeling as the abstraction that enables this.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest distinction is that, in the earlier era, we had a general recipe, but we were still building fairly specialized systems. You could use deep learning for speech recognition, image classification, or translation, but you would typically train a different model, with a different dataset and a different objective, for each task. The methodology was general; the resulting model wasn’t necessarily general.

With the current generation, we’re increasingly putting that generality into the model itself. You train one model, and then you can ask it to do many different things, including things you didn’t explicitly train it to do. That changes how you interact with it: instead of collecting a dataset and training a new system for every problem, you can describe the problem, give a few examples, and see whether the capability is already there.

Of course, it’s a continuum. The earlier work gave us the ingredients for this. But that shift—from a general learning algorithm to a model with broadly useful capabilities—is, to me, the important one.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a general deep learning recipe producing task-specific systems with current models that hold broadly useful capabilities, placing generality in the trained model.

r002.rationale: It says one model can do many tasks, but does not identify language modeling as the abstraction enabling this.
